Those things and others, including the voice performances, made the short special. But Jones liked to credit one element and one person in particular with its success. He pointed to Maurice Noble, designer of the colors and layouts.

And every shot of it required Noble’s touch. “Without Maurice Noble, who excited, moved and stimulated us all,” Jones wrote, “that film could not have been made.”

Maurice Noble was one of the top mid-century cartoon designers. But he wasn’t a member or a fan of UPA. “I don’t believe I was influenced by UPA at all. ... I think UPA outsmarted itself in overdesigning,” he said. The UPA designers, for their part, didn’t seem to like him, either.

I am a great believer in the idea that color and visual impact have a lot to do with the response of the audience. I would play for dramatic impact in both design and color, in terms of putting over a story point. No background is any good unless it’s appropriate to the given situation or mood of the thing that’s being portrayed.
This functional aspect of Noble’s work was something Jones loved and often glowed about:

He had great staging techniques, and he understood what very few background men do understand — and actually very many live-action people don’t seem to understand it in the graphics area: that the purpose of a great designer is to design an arena where the actor can perform. When Noble took over, he scrapped that direction in favor of “super-grand opera” with “super, colossal settings,” over-the-top enough to spoof the medium.

The upcoming book Nizo Yamamoto: Art for Animation collects the work of the great Japanese background artist. It’s the first English book about him, done by the folks behind Anime Architecture.
In America, Phil Tippett’s studio just closed with a massive auction, after almost 40 years in business.
The Palestinian rap group BLTNM started an animated series on YouTube, produced by the studio Stereo.
A film by Ukrainian director Volodymyr Dakhno, behind the Cossacks series, has been restored and will screen at the Linoleum festival next month.
In America, Amid Amidi revealed details about his immense, heavily illustrated Ward Kimball biography, which is nearly complete and scheduled to hit Kickstarter next year.

An in-depth behind-the-scenes video about the Japanese series Jaadugar is up on YouTube.

In Russia, there’s been a large uproar over a police crackdown on a girl’s playground drawings of the characters from KikoRiki, an animated series. The company behind KikoRiki responded by inviting her for a studio visit.
Finally: a look into The Good Soldier Švejk (1954–1955) by Jiří Trnka.
That’s our issue for today! Hope you’ve enjoyed. We’re closing out with personal comments from the two of us:

John: The loss of Curry and Cullen, and the end of Phil Tippett’s studio, were tough headlines to read this week. Those are all major legacies, and I’m left wondering about the future. A friend messaged me that Tim Curry was one of those irreplaceable people, a type who isn’t even made anymore. I think about the path he took and whether the infrastructure exists now for people to do what he did. The masters are getting older, and all of us in the younger generations are on next. Even if they’re impossible acts to follow, we owe it to them to try somehow.

Jules: The control and depth of Curry’s voice performances are things I associate with actors of his generation, many of whom had education and experience in live theater. So many things go into the formation of artists: the traditions they’re trained in, the prevailing taste and artistic theories of the moment, the economic incentives around them, the projects available to work on, the other artists they happen to meet. Like how Hayao Miyazaki was so heavily formed by his peers, whether in his early years in the Toei union or during his TV work with Takahata. Sometimes it can feel like artists in previous eras benefited from circumstances that have long since changed. Whatever circumstances we happen to find ourselves in today, I believe that serious discussion, study, analysis and collaboration can go a long way in helping us keep up.
Until next time!
